section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the two aspects of the revelation of the King in the field during Elul—that it reaches even the most distant, yet does not awaken them but only gives power—through the analogy of a king in the field versus a king in his palace.
section.t: And in order to explain the two aforementioned matters regarding the revelation of the King’s countenance in Elul—that the revelation of Elul is for each and every one, even for the most distant,
and that nevertheless the revelation does not awaken the person and is only a giving of power—the maamar continues,
that the revelation of the King’s countenance in Elul is analogous to a king in the field.
For from the distinctions between a king in the field and a king in his palace come the two matters.
Regarding the level of the revelation,
the essential revelation of the king in his beauty
(your eyes shall behold)
is in the palace of his kingdom,
when he is in royal garments and the royal crown,
unlike when he is in the field.
But the revelation itself is primarily when he is in the field.
For when he is in his royal palace, none may enter except by permission and only the choicest of the people and select individuals,
and when he is in the field,
all are permitted
[and able]
to greet him, whoever wishes,
and the king receives them all with a pleasant countenance and shows a smiling face to everyone.
And so it is in the analogy,

that the revelation of Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur, and likewise the Ten Days of Repentance in general, which is analogous to a king in his palace, is in a manner that the revelation awakens the person,
like a king in his palace
(in royal garments and the royal crown),
which instills awe and fear.
But in order for a person to feel the revelation of Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur,
it is
(primarily)
after the preceding service in the month of Elul,
through which he becomes one of the choicest of the people and the select individuals who enter the king’s palace.
And the revelation of Elul, which is analogous to a king in the field,
is in a manner that the revelation does not awaken the person and is only a giving of power for service,
but the giving of power for service through this revelation is for each and every one, even for the most distant.
Like a king in the field,
for when the king is in this state, he does not instill awe and fear.
And especially regarding those who are in the field,
who are on a low level.
And moreover,
when the king is in this state,
he does not even awaken a desire to greet him.
And this is what the maamar precisely states: “whoever wishes to go out to greet him,”
that their going out to greet the king is from their own will.
Rather, the giving of power to greet the king is through the king being in the field.
For then,
(when he is in the field)
there is permission and ability for each and every one to greet the king.

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section raises questions about the analogy of the king in the field, specifically why the maamar adds that the king receives everyone with a pleasant and smiling countenance, and the need to understand the two distinct expressions.
section.t: And it must be understood,
that seemingly, in order to explain that the revelation of Elul
(and the giving of power through the revelation)
is for each and every one,
it would only be relevant that when the king is in the field, all who wish are permitted and able to greet him,
so why does it add that the king receives them all with a pleasant countenance and shows a smiling face to everyone?
And especially, that the king receiving them all with a pleasant countenance and showing them a smiling face is the drawing down and revelation from above that comes after the service,
and it is not understood,
that the drawing down and revelation after the service
(and my Beloved is mine)
is during the Ten Days of Repentance,
while the analogy of the king in the field is an explanation of the revelation of Elul, which is
(a giving of power and)
before the service.
Also, the two matters—that he receives them with a pleasant countenance and that he shows them a smiling face—need to be understood.
And also,
that regarding receiving them it says “with a pleasant countenance,” and regarding showing them it says “a smiling face.”

section.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the innovation of the revelation of the King’s countenance in Elul lies in two aspects: it requires only the acceptance of the yoke of heaven, and it reaches even those in the desert, giving them power to leave the desert and greet the king.
section.t: And the explanation of this can be given by first prefacing that the novelty in the revelation of the King’s countenance in Elul, relative to the revelation on Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur, is in two matters.
That in order to receive the revelation of Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur, it is through lofty service
(the choicest of the people and select individuals),
and in order to receive the revelation of Elul, only the greeting of the king is needed,
which in the analogy is the arousal of accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven.
And another novelty in the revelation of Elul is that the revelation is also for those who are in the desert
—for matters that are contrary to His will.
And this is also understood from the fact that the essential revelation of the King’s countenance in Elul is a giving of power for repentance,
for repentance in its simple sense is for undesirable matters
(the aspect of desert),
and the essence of repentance is for casting off the yoke,
from which it is understood,
that the revelation of Elul is also for those who are at the ultimate distance.
And what the maamar says, that the revelation of Elul is in the field
(and not in the desert),
is
because the revelation of the King’s countenance is
(not in the desert itself,
for in matters that are contrary to the will of God,
it is not possible for there to be a revelation of Divinity,
but rather)
in the Jews who are in the desert,
and the revelation within them is the giving of power to leave the desert for the field to greet the king.
And based on this, it can be said,
that what the maamar says, that the king receives them all with a pleasant countenance,
the intention in emphasizing “all of them” is,

that even those who only wish to greet the king but are captive in the hands of their evil inclination, and even when a desire to repent and accept the yoke of the kingdom of heaven is aroused in them, it does not come into actuality,
even them he receives with a pleasant countenance,
and this arouses in them a strong and powerful desire to greet the king,
and through this desire they overcome the obstacles and delays.
